extracted.intended_audience: lay first-aid providers, non-medical caregivers, people in places without immediate surgical help
extracted.subtask_description: Practical first-aid recognition and temporary treatment instructions for fractures and common dislocations, intended for non-surgeons to use until skilled medical help is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken jaw: diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Owing to displacement of the fragments there is a difference in the level of the teeth or line of the teeth, or both, at the place where the fracture occurs. Also one or more of the teeth are usually loosened at this point. In addition, unusual movement of the fragments may be detected as well as a grating sound on manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for difference in tooth level, loosened teeth, abnormal movement, and grating sound; avoid excessive manipulation except gentle checks; these signs distinguish fracture from other injuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken jaw: first-aid treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The broken fragments should be pressed into place with the fingers, and retained temporarily with a four-tailed bandage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feed through a glass tube using milk, broths, thin gruels. Use a mouth wash four times daily (menthol 1/2 grain; thymol 1/2 grain; boric acid 20 grains; water 8 oz). Tie jaw with a four-tailed bandage up against upper jaw for a week; protect thumbs when reducing (see dislocation rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoulder-blade fracture: first-aid rule & immobilization
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no displacement. Bandage fingers, forearm, and arm of affected side, and put this arm in sling. Fasten slung arm to body with many turns of a bandage, which holds forearm against chest and arm against side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bandage forearm and arm from below upward, sling forearm bent at a right angle across front of body, encircle body and arm from shoulder to elbow with a wide bandage applied under the sling; use straps carried over shoulders to prevent slipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arm fracture: diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: In fracture of the arm between the shoulder and elbow, swelling and shortening may give rise to deformity. Pain and abnormal motion are symptoms, while a grating sound may be detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid manipulating the arm to elicit grating; look for swelling, shortening, deformity, pain, abnormal motion, and 'black and blue' discoloration from ruptured vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arm fracture: first-aid setting and splinting
rubrics_metrics.description: Put forearm and hand in sling. The bone is put in place by grasping the patient's elbow and pulling directly down in line with the arm, while an assistant steadies and pulls up the shoulder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a wedge-shaped pad from armpit to elbow secured by adhesive plaster or bandage; apply three padded splints (front, outside, back) from shoulder to elbow secured with adhesive plaster; surround with wide bandage from shoulder to elbow and support wrist in a narrow sling (not over 2 in wide). Union usually 4–6 weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forearm fracture: diagnostic signs
rubrics_metrics.description: When both bones are broken there is marked deformity caused by displacement of fragments, unusual motion, and possibly a grating sound; when only one is broken there may be tenderness and irregularity of bone surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As with other fractures, avoid excessive manipulation to test for grating; use steadiness and careful observation for deformity, tenderness, and abnormal motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forearm fracture: reduction and splinting
rubrics_metrics.description: Set bones in proper place by pulling steadily on wrist while assistant holds back the upper part of the forearm. If successful, put padded splints one on each side, front and back, and wind a bandage about the whole thing to hold it immovably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position elbow at right angle with forearm horizontally across chest, hand palm toward body and thumb uppermost. Use two quarter-inch-thick wooden splints covered with padding: one on back of hand/forearm, one on palm/front. Secure with strips of adhesive plaster (upper ends, above wrist, around hand) and a bandage from wrist to elbow; support in wide sling. Allow ~4 weeks for union; for compound fractures follow compound-fracture protocol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colles' (wrist) fracture: recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Break of lower end of the bone on thumb side of wrist; a hump or swelling appears on back of wrist and a deep crease is seen just above the hand in front; whole hand displaced toward thumb side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often no abnormal motion or grating can be detected because fragments are jammed; this injury is common in elderly patients who fall on palm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colles' (wrist) fracture: treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Until medical aid is obtained, apply same sort of splints as for fractured forearm. If deformity is not relieved a stiff and painful joint usually persists; surgeon may need to pull fragments apart under ether to remedy deformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporary splinting is essential; advise prompt surgical reduction if deformity persists—full correction may be impossible in elderly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finger/hand bone fracture: first-aid rule and splinting
rubrics_metrics.description: Set fragments by pulling on finger and pressing fragments into position; apply a thin wooden splint (cigar box) padded, extending from wrist to beyond fingertip, and retain with adhesive plaster and bandage; put forearm and hand in sling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify by sunken knuckle on closed fist, tenderness, abnormal motion, and grating; place additional padding in palm over fracture; allow ~3 weeks for firm union and avoid use of hand for a month; thumb fractures: splint applied along back of thumb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hip fracture: recognition and measurement for shortening
rubrics_metrics.description: Patient unable to rise or walk; foot of injured side turned outward and leg may be apparently shorter; pain on movement and inability to raise heel. Measure from hip-bone to ankle prominence; shortening less than 1/2 inch is not important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fragments often impacted so no grating; avoid manipulation—gentle handling only. Keep patient quiet on hard mattress with small pillow under knee and limb steadied by pillows until surgeon arrives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thigh-bone (femur) fracture: first-aid preparation and splinting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare long padded splints (armpit to ankle; crotch to knee; inside leg; front thigh) and apply after pulling steadily on the leg to relax muscles and bring fragments into line; fasten splints with straps and a wide band around body from armpit to hips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use wide padding over ribs under outside splint; draw splints together and secure with multiple straps (above ankle, below knee, above knee, mid-thigh, upper thigh); when patient can be bedded, outer/back/front splints may suffice; permanent setting requires surgeon with anaesthesia and subsequent traction (15–20 lb) to prevent muscle contraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kneepan (patella) fracture: immediate immobilization and swelling control
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediate pain and enormous swelling; separated fragments may be felt; splint from upper thigh to above ankle padded to fill space behind knee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply padded splint attached with adhesive-plaster straps (upper, lower, just below knee). Bind a flat dry sponge over knee and keep wet with cold water or use ice; put patient to bed with leg elevated and supported by a cradle to keep clothes off limb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fracture of leg (between knee and ankle): cautious handling and pillow dressing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pain, angular deformity or false joint, swelling and tenderness; two bones (tibia and fibula) may be broken with displacement and grating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handle very carefully to avoid creating an open (compound) fracture. If surgeon unavailable, use Scudder pillow-dressing: place large soft pillow under leg, bring pillow edges up and pin, place three wooden splints (inner, outer, back) over pillow and leg from sole to above knee, and secure with four straps (one above knee, one above ankle, two between). Keep leg elevated; union in adults 1–2 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ankle-joint fracture: recognition and temporary splinting
rubrics_metrics.description: One or both bones of leg may be broken just above ankle. Foot generally pushed or bent outward and displaced backward on leg; inner ankle prominence marked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May mimic sprain; in fracture foot drops back to displaced state. Temporarily return foot to usual position and apply side splints and a back splint as for leg fracture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound (open) fracture: immediate cleansing and sterile handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Wound communicates with the break either from external violence or from bone projecting through skin, allowing germs to enter and making condition much more serious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shave hair around wound, wash with warm water and soap using clean cotton, boil absorbent cotton or cloth and use boiled water (cooled) to irrigate wound with boiled cotton; operator must thoroughly wash hands and avoid touching anything but the boiled water vessel and patient. Spread boiled cotton (untouched) wet over wound, cover with clean dry cotton and bandage. Then apply splints as for simple fracture. If bone projects, it may be replaced after cleansing by pulling limb in line; maintain sterility throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: General fracture handling: do no harm and when in doubt treat as fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive manipulation; greatest danger lies in the desire to do too much. When in doubt as to the existence of a fracture always treat the limb as if a fracture were present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt side-to-side or back-and-forth movement to elicit grating; gentle traction in line of limb is acceptable to align; prioritize immobilization, padding, elevation, and transport; know that time to union varies (weeks to months).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dislocation vs sprain vs fracture: distinguishing features
rubrics_metrics.description: A dislocation is an injury where bones forming a joint are forced out of place and remain out; in a sprain bones may be momentarily displaced but return to place; in fracture near a joint there is usually increased movement in a new direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dislocated joint cannot be moved except within narrow limits; a dislocated part stays in place after reduction; avoid unnecessary attempts at reduction if skilled help is available; instructions are meant for those without immediate surgical attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jaw dislocation (reduction): safety and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect your thumbs (thick leather gloves or bound bandage). Assistant steadies patient from behind; operator presses downward and backward with thumbs on back teeth while chin is grasped and raised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate method: place a cork as far back as possible between back teeth and have patient bite down to pry jaw back. After reduction tie jaw with a four-tailed bandage against upper jaw for a week; feed liquids through tube so patient need not open mouth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shoulder dislocation (Stimson's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Place patient on injured side on canvas cot raised; allow injured arm to hang downward through a hole in the cot with hand not touching the floor; attach a ten-pound weight to the wrist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gradual traction produced by the weight generally brings the shoulder back into place without pain within about six minutes. Recognize shoulder dislocation by loss of shoulder fullness, arm held slightly away from body, and inability to place hand on opposite shoulder without pain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knee dislocation (simple reduction rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put patient on back; flex thigh on abdomen and hold it there; grasp leg below knee, twist it back and forth, and straighten knee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knee dislocations are rare but easily reduced; proceed with caution and avoid forceful or injudicious manipulation if surgeon is available.
